A pod is a backend: a website or an app can read and write its records through the same doors, permissions and
governance as the Synap apps.

## Pick how your site connects

| Your site | Use | Credential |
|---|---|---|
| Shows what you published from your pod (a share, a form, a project published as a site) to anyone | `@synap-core/sdk/public` | None: the public token of what you published |
| Lets each visitor connect **their own** pod and work on their records | `@synap-core/sdk/connect` (this tutorial) | The visitor's consent; the token stays on your server |
| Runs on your own server against your own pod (a portfolio, an internal tool) | [`@synap-core/hub-rest-client`](/docs/build/sdk#scripts-and-agents-with-an-api-key) | An [API key](/docs/build/api-keys) kept on the server |
| Runs where the person is already signed in to the pod (same domain) | The typed client in [`@synap-core/sdk`](/docs/build/sdk) | The person's sign-in session |

Never put an API key in code that runs in the browser.

## Build an app people connect to their pod

You will build a small notes app. A visitor enters their pod's address; their pod shows a consent screen that lists
what the app asks for and lets them choose which spaces it may use; the app then lists their notes and creates new
ones.

`@synap-core/sdk/connect` handles the sign-in for you: the OAuth flow with PKCE, the checks on the pod's answers, the
token kept in a sealed, HTTP-only cookie on your server, and its renewal. It is server-only and throws if it is loaded
in a browser. It uses Web-standard `Request` and `Response`, so it works in Next.js route handlers and other
frameworks; this tutorial uses the Next.js App Router.

### What you need

- A Next.js 16 app (Next.js 16 names its middleware `proxy.ts`).
- An https address for it, for example `https://notes.example.com`. A real pod only accepts an app served over https;
  in development, use a tunnel.
- A pod to connect to, [hosted](/docs/start/cloud-quickstart) or [self-hosted](/docs/start/self-host-quickstart).

<Steps>
<Step>

### Install the SDK and set two variables

```bash
npm install @synap-core/sdk
```

```bash title=".env.local"
SYNAP_APP_URL=https://notes.example.com
SYNAP_APP_SESSION_SECRET=<at least 32 random characters>
```

`SYNAP_APP_URL` is your app's origin: no path, no trailing slash, a domain name rather than an IP address.
`SYNAP_APP_SESSION_SECRET` seals the cookie that holds the connection. Keep both server-side, never in a
`NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable.

</Step>
<Step>

### Describe your app

```ts title="lib/synap.ts"
import { createPodAppAuth } from "@synap-core/sdk/connect";

export const synap = createPodAppAuth({
  appUrl: process.env.SYNAP_APP_URL!,
  clientName: "My notes",
  requests: [
    { permission: "entity.note.read", reason: "Show your notes" },
    { permission: "entity.note.create", reason: "Save the notes you write here" },
  ],
  secret: process.env.SYNAP_APP_SESSION_SECRET!,
});
```

Each request is one permission, written `<subject>.<kind>.<action>` as in
[API key grants](/docs/build/api-keys#grants-what-a-key-may-touch), with the sentence the consent screen shows. Ask
for exactly what the app does: wildcards are refused, and the person sees every line. The SDK refuses at startup what
the pod would refuse at sign-in.

</Step>
<Step>

### Mount the sign-in routes

Each route file re-exports one handler:

```ts title="app/.well-known/synap-client.json/route.ts"
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";
export const GET = synap.handlers.clientMetadata;
```

```ts title="app/api/synap/connect/route.ts"
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";
export const POST = synap.handlers.connect;
```

```ts title="app/api/synap/callback/route.ts"
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";
export const GET = synap.handlers.callback;
```

```ts title="app/api/synap/disconnect/route.ts"
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";
export const POST = synap.handlers.disconnect;
```

`/.well-known/synap-client.json` describes your app to the pod. Its URL is your app's client ID, so there is nothing
to register on the pod beforehand. `connect` and `disconnect` accept only a `POST` from your own pages.

</Step>
<Step>

### Renew the connection before each page

A server component cannot set cookies, so the connection is renewed in `proxy.ts`, before the page renders:

```ts title="proxy.ts"
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";

export async function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  const outcome = await synap.refreshIfNeeded(request);
  const headers = new Headers(request.headers);
  if (outcome.cookieHeader !== null) headers.set("cookie", outcome.cookieHeader);
  const response = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers } });
  for (const cookie of outcome.setCookies) response.headers.append("Set-Cookie", cookie);
  return response;
}

export const config = {
  matcher: [
    {
      source: "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|api/synap/|\\.well-known/|.*\\.\\w+$).*)",
      missing: [
        { type: "header", key: "next-router-prefetch" },
        { type: "header", key: "purpose", value: "prefetch" },
      ],
    },
  ],
};
```

`refreshIfNeeded` renews the token only in its last five minutes. Forwarding `cookieHeader` lets the page see the
renewed token in the same request. The matcher skips static files, the sign-in routes and router prefetches.

</Step>
<Step>

### Add a connect page

```tsx title="app/connect/page.tsx"
export default function ConnectPage() {
  return (
    <form method="post" action="/api/synap/connect">
      <label>
        Your pod address <input name="pod" placeholder="pod.example.com" required />
      </label>
      <button type="submit">Connect</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

The form posts the pod's address (`https://` is added when it is missing). The visitor goes to their pod, approves,
and comes back to `/`. A sign-in that fails comes back with an `error` code in the query: on `/connect` when it could
not start, on `/connect/result` when it failed on the way back.

</Step>
<Step>

### Read the visitor's notes

```tsx title="app/page.tsx"
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";
import { addNote } from "./actions";

export default async function Home() {
  const connection = await synap.readConnection((await headers()).get("cookie"));
  if (!connection) redirect("/connect");

  const pod = synap.client(connection);
  const notes = await pod.listEntities({ profileSlug: "note", limit: 50 });
  if (!notes.ok) return <p>Could not read your notes ({notes.error.code}).</p>;

  return (
    <main>
      <form action={addNote}>
        <input name="title" required />
        <button type="submit">Add note</button>
      </form>
      <ul>
        {notes.data.map((note) => (
          <li key={note.id}>{note.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}
```

Calls return a result instead of throwing: `{ ok: true, data }`, or `{ ok: false, error }` whose `error.code` says what
happened, such as `expired` (connect again), `forbidden` (the person did not grant it), `rate_limited` or
`pod_unreachable`. The app sees only the spaces the person chose; without `workspaceId`, `listEntities` reads all of
them.

</Step>
<Step>

### Write, and expect a proposal

```ts title="app/actions.ts"
"use server";
import { headers } from "next/headers";
import { redirect } from "next/navigation";
import { synap } from "@/lib/synap";

export async function addNote(form: FormData) {
  const connection = await synap.readConnection((await headers()).get("cookie"));
  if (!connection) redirect("/connect");

  const pod = synap.client(connection);
  const space = pod.spaces()[0]; // a space the person granted
  if (!space) redirect("/connect");

  const result = await pod.post("/entities", {
    profileSlug: "note",
    title: String(form.get("title")),
    workspaceId: space.workspaceId,
  });

  if (!result.ok) redirect(`/?failed=${result.error.code}`);
  if (result.status === "proposed") redirect(`/?review=${encodeURIComponent(result.reviewUrl)}`);
  redirect("/?saved=1");
}
```

Every create names a space the person granted. A connected app acts as its own agent, one that asks first, so its
writes come back as `status: "proposed"` with a `reviewUrl`, and the person approves them in their pod. That is a success: show
"Sent to your pod for review" with the link, and never retry it. (`pod.actsAs` is `"agent"` for every app except
Synap's official ones, whose writes apply directly.)

</Step>
</Steps>

### Test without a pod

`@synap-core/sdk/testing` has a mock pod, `createMockAuthServer()`, for development and tests. With
`allowInsecureLoopback: true`, `createPodAppAuth` accepts it on `http://localhost`; a real pod, even a local one, still
needs your app on https.

### Going further

The connection client has typed reads beyond `listEntities`: `getEntity`, `getEntityConnections`, `getDocument`,
`getFileUrl` (a signed link to a file) and `listPendingProposals` (what waits for the person's review; needs
`proposal.read`). `spaces()` and `can(permission, workspaceId)` let a page adapt to what was granted. `pod.actions`
asks the person's own tools to do something for them, such as publishing a post, after they approve it (needs
`capability.<intent>.run`). [Pod-app sign-in](/docs/build/pod-app-sign-in) is the reference for every option,
result and error code, and the `AGENTS.md` file shipped in the npm package documents every rule.

## A public site

To show what you published from your pod, with no sign-in at all:

```ts
import { createPublicClient } from "@synap-core/sdk/public";

const pod = createPublicClient({ podUrl: "https://pod.example.com" });
const page = await pod.listCollection("<site token>", "<collection key>");
if (page.ok) console.log(page.data);
```

The client reads a public share (`readShare`), a form (`getForm`, `submitForm`), or a project you published as a site
(`getSite`, `listCollection`, `getRecord`). Publishing a site creates its token, shown once to the person who
publishes it. The same entry has helpers that turn what it reads into safe page models: render pod content through
them, never as raw HTML.
